one_liner: Python-to-C/C++ compiler; hand-typed Cython kernels ran 30-190x faster than CPython 3.10, untyped code about 1x.
what_it_does: Cython compiles Python and its own superset language (.pyx with cdef declarations of C types, structs, pointers and C functions) into C or C++ source that builds into CPython extension modules, or with --embed into a standalone executable linked against libpython. Plain Python modules usually compile unchanged, but the large speedups come from adding C types (in .pyx syntax or pure-Python-mode annotations) to hot code. It is also the standard way to wrap C and C++ libraries for Python through 'cdef extern from' declarations.
how_it_is_fast: Typed code is lowered to plain C: cdef int/double variables, C structs, malloc'd arrays and cdef functions compile to unboxed arithmetic and direct C calls with no bytecode dispatch, reference counting or dynamic lookup, which gcc then optimizes (-O3 -march=native in the benchmark). Untyped code still goes through the CPython C-API on PyObjects, so it saves only interpreter dispatch overhead. 'cdef extern from' lets a kernel call a C library directly; the pidigits kernel calls GMP's mpz functions.
when_to_use: Numeric inner loops on doubles and ints that you are willing to annotate with C types (n-body, mandelbrot, spectral norm, matrix multiply style kernels), where the suite shows 30-190x over CPython.
Wrapping existing C or C++ libraries for Python, or calling them from hot paths (generated code can be C++ with --cplus).
Speeding up a module while staying on CPython with full access to its C-extension ecosystem, which PyPy and Codon do not fully offer.
Incremental optimization: compile unchanged Python first, then add types only where profiling shows the time goes.
Shipping a single executable that embeds the interpreter (cython --embed, as this benchmark did).
when_not_to_use: You expect large gains on unmodified Python: the suite's barely typed ports gain little or lose (regexdna 6.1 s vs CPython 5.2 s, knucleotide 8.33 vs 8.41, fasta 6.81 vs 8.65).
The time is already spent in C-implemented builtins or stdlib modules (re, dict, str operations), where removing interpreter dispatch saves almost nothing.
You cannot add a C compiler and per-platform binary wheels to the build, or need a pure-Python package.
You build against the Limited API (abi3) for speed-critical code: open issue #6741 reports Limited-API builds 2x to 12x slower than regular Cython builds on its benchmarks.
A JIT on unmodified code is acceptable: PyPy reached 0.54 s on mandelbrot and 0.36 s on matmul in the same suite without type annotations.

integration.form: module (build-time compiler, pip install Cython, that emits C/C++ for extension modules or embedded executables)
integration.dependencies: a C or C++ compiler and the target Python's headers/libpython; Cython itself is needed only at build time; GMP in the benchmark's pidigits kernel only
integration.min_toolchain: Python 3.9+ for current Cython (setup.py python_requires); C99 compiler for generated code since 3.1; the benchmark used Cython 0.29.30 with gcc 12.2.0
integration.platforms: any platform with a CPython C toolchain (setup.py lists OS Independent); classifiers also list PyPy and GraalPy
integration.thread_safety: Generated code follows CPython's GIL model; nogil sections release the GIL for pure C code, and the 3.2-3.3 changelogs carry fixes for free-threading builds
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — most Python modules compile unchanged into extension modules with the same behaviour, but the measured speedups need Cython-specific C typing, i.e. different source

gotchas: The benchmark's .pyx files are C written in Cython syntax, not compiled Python: binarytrees, nbody, fannkuchredux, matmul and spectralnorm use C structs or malloc'd arrays (fannkuchredux, matmul and spectralnorm never free them, so memory grows over the five in-process repetitions; matmul MaxMem 84.5 MB vs 16.6 MB for C), and Cython ties or beats the suite's own C entries on five kernels (fannkuchredux 0.13 s vs C 0.21 s uses a cheaper permutation loop than test.c).

pidigits' 3.6x (1.73 s vs 6.17 s) comes from calling GMP directly (cdef extern from "gmp.h", linked with -lgmp) against CPython's built-in integers; it measures a C bignum library, not compiled Python.

The .pyx files rely on Cython 0.29's language_level=2 default (Python 2 print statements in pidigits, binarytrees and spectralnorm); Cython 3.0 (2023-07-17) changed the default to 3str and 3.1 to 3 and dropped Python 2.7-3.7, so they do not build unchanged on current Cython without a language_level=2 directive.

Timing is the best of up to 5 repetitions inside one process, read from each program's own time.time() report, so start-up and the 0.8-2.6 s Cython+gcc compile are excluded; output correctness is checked only on small debug inputs. Upstream also has open slowdown reports: #6597 (compiled try/except plus list.append 48% slower than CPython, Cython 3.0.11) and #6710 (performance regressions in 3.1).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Cython over PyPy, GraalPy or Codon when you must stay on CPython with its C extensions, and over mypyc or Nuitka (which compile type-hinted or plain Python for 1.5-5x at best) when you are willing to write C-level types to get C speed or need to wrap C/C++ code; pick PyPy or Codon instead when the code should stay unmodified Python.
verified_claims_summary: In kostya/jit-benchmarks round 1 (2023-02-28, AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, Docker on Ubuntu 22.10), Cython 0.29.30 --embed output built with gcc 12.2.0 -O3 -march=native ran hand-typed .pyx ports against idiomatic CPython 3.10.7 scripts: binarytrees 0.81 vs 73.15 s, mandelbrot 0.43 vs 37.52 s, nbody 0.56 vs 53.72 s, spectralnorm 0.11 vs 20.69 s, matmul 0.39 vs 22.73 s, fannkuchredux 0.13 vs 4.04 s and pidigits (GMP) 1.73 vs 6.17 s (best in-process times). Lightly typed ports were level or slower: fasta 6.81 vs 8.65 s, knucleotide 8.33 vs 8.41 s, regexdna 6.1 vs 5.2 s.
status_note: Actively maintained (3.3.0 released 2026-08-22 per CHANGES.rst, Apache-2.0, 10.9k stars) and a build-time-only dependency, but the measured versions (Cython 0.29, Python 3.10) are two major releases old and the benchmark's .pyx files need language_level=2 to build on Cython 3.x.
